facts.statement: Fossils of Losillasaurus have also been found in the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal.
facts.quote: It is also known from the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal.

facts.statement: The type species Losillasaurus giganteus was discovered in the Villar del Arzobispo Formation in Valencia and formally described by Casanovas, Santafé, and Sanz in 2001.
facts.quote: The type species, Losillasaurus giganteus, was discovered in the Villar del Arzobispo Formation in Valencia, and formally described by Casanovas, Santafé, and Sanz in 2001.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a subadult skeleton including part of a skull, vertebrae, limb bones, sternal plates, and pelvic elements.
facts.quote: The holotype material is from a subadult and includes part of a skull; complete cervical, dorsal, sacral, and caudal vertebrae as well as several fragments; skeletal elements from the limbs including a humerus, ulna, radius, and metacarpal; sternal plates; and from the pelvis: the ilium, ischium, and pubis.

facts.statement: Research indicates that Losillasaurus possessed heart-shaped teeth and exhibited heterodonty, a variation in tooth types within the skull.
facts.quote: According to Rafael Royo-Torres et al., the specimen helps scientists to understand tooth variation, allows the positioning of isolated heart-shaped teeth in the skull and demonstrates heterodonty in Turiasauria.

facts.statement: The humerus of the type specimen measures 143 cm, which is within 20% of the size of Paralititan despite coming from a subadult.
facts.quote: The humerus is 143 cm long, which despite being from a subadult specimen is within 20% of the size of Paralititan.

facts.statement: The largest estimated Losillasaurus would have measured 25 meters in length and weighed approximately 47 tonnes.
facts.quote: The largest Losillasaurus would have measured 25 m in length and weighed about 47 tonnes.

facts.statement: Additional specimens of L. giganteus were described in 2019 and 2020, including a single anterior caudal vertebra and a partial skull with teeth.
facts.quote: Several specimens of L. giganteus were described in 2019 and 2020 - one such specimen (SHN 180) consists of a single anterior caudal vertebra, while another (the holotype) consists of a partial skull with teeth and partial postcranial skeleton.

facts.statement: Losillasaurus is classified within the unranked family Turiasauria.
Losillasaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 154 to 145 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Jurásico Tardío, hace aproximadamente 154-145 millones de años, en el Titoniense, en lo que hoy es Europa.

facts.statement: The type species was discovered in the Los Serranos comarca in Valencia, Spain, within the Collado Sandstone and Clay Formation.
facts.quote: La especie tipo de Losillasaurus giganteus fue descubierta en la comarca de Los Serranos (Valencia, España), en la Formación Arenas y arcillas del Collado, y formalmente descrito por Casanovas, Santafé y Sanz en 2001.

facts.statement: The genus is characterized by the dimensions and shape of the neural spines on the proximal caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: El género caracterizado por la dimensión y la forma de las espinas vértebrales de las vértebras caudales próximales.

facts.statement: Although estimates vary, Losillasaurus was large, with a humerus length of 143 cm suggesting a total length of about 25 meters.
facts.quote: Aunque no hay estimaciones de buena calidad, Losillasaurus era grande. El húmero media alrededor de 143 centímetros de largo, el cual a pesar de ser de un espécimen subadulto está dentro del 20% del tamaño Paralititan., estimándose unos 25 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The time range for Losillasaurus is the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages, from 154.8 to 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (154.8 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of Losillasaurus is Turiasauria.

rejected.quote: Losillasaurus (meaning "Losilla lizard") is a genus of turiasaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic and possibly Early Cretaceous (Kimmeridgian-?Berriasian) of southeastern Spain.
